content: Leprosy, also known as Hansen’s disease, is an infectious disease caused by a bacterium. If left untreated, it can result in severe complications, including permanent disability and disfigurement. However, leprosy is curable with a complete course of multidrug therapy (MDT). The disease is primarily transmitted through prolonged close contact with an untreated individual. When an infected person sneezes or coughs, the bacteria are released into the air and can be inhaled by others. While most individuals have a natural immunity to the disease, some may develop leprosy after many years of exposure. Close contacts of a leprosy patient, such as family members, neighbors, or colleagues who have spent significant time with the patient (e.g., 20 hours per week for at least three months per year), may also be at risk of infection. To prevent the development of leprosy in such individuals, a single dose of the antibiotic rifampicin can be administered. Rifampicin is highly effective in killing the bacteria before the disease manifests. Research has demonstrated, and the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends, that a single dose of rifampicin (SDR) given to contacts without symptoms can significantly reduce their risk of developing leprosy. Now that you have started treatment, you are no longer infectious, and you will be cured. However, to protect your family, neighbors, colleagues, or friends from developing leprosy, we recommend screening your close contacts for signs and symptoms of the disease. If they show no signs of leprosy, they can be offered a single dose of rifampicin to prevent the disease. This intervention is safe and effective. By agreeing to this, you allow us to disclose your diagnosis to your contacts so that we can screen and protect them. If you consent, please sign the form to confirm your agreement to disclose your diagnosis and allow us to trace your contacts. For individuals who are close contacts of a leprosy patient, it is important to understand the risks and preventive measures. Since you live in an area where leprosy is endemic or have spent significant time with a patient, you may have been exposed to the bacteria. Although there is currently no test to confirm whether you are infected, there is a possibility that you could develop leprosy in the future, even after many years. To reduce this risk, we offer you a single dose of rifampicin, which is a highly effective antibiotic that kills the bacteria before the disease develops. This single-dose treatment reduces the risk of developing leprosy by more than 50%. Before administering rifampicin, we will need to examine your body to rule out any signs of leprosy and ask you some questions to ensure there are no contraindications for taking the medication. Rifampicin is very safe when given as a single dose. The most common side effect is a temporary red discoloration of urine, which resolves within a few hours. Rarely, other side effects such as stomach upset, flu-like symptoms, or jaundice may occur. If you experience any of these symptoms, you should immediately report to the nearest health facility for appropriate treatment. If you agree to be screened for signs and symptoms of leprosy and to take a single dose of rifampicin to reduce your risk of developing the disease, please sign the consent form. This intervention is a critical step in preventing the spread of leprosy and protecting your health. To effectively reduce the number of new leprosy cases among contacts, public health programs can choose between two approaches: treating all identified leprosy cases without providing chemoprophylaxis to contacts or administering chemoprophylaxis to all contacts while treating only a subset of leprosy cases. The latter approach, which involves providing single-dose rifampicin to contacts, is the most efficient and widely recommended strategy. This document provides detailed guidance on implementing contact screening and chemoprophylaxis with single-dose rifampicin. It includes step-by-step instructions on counseling and obtaining consent, identifying and listing index cases, tracing and screening contacts, and administering prophylactic drugs. Additionally, it outlines the managerial aspects of planning, training, supervision, and drug management necessary for successful implementation of the program.
